thread.title: Paul Wick on Who Wins the IT Spending Race

author: barrons.com
title: Paul Wick on Who Wins the IT Spending Race
text:
Paul Wick Photo: Jeremy Liebman July 13, 2018 8:24 p.m. ET Barron’s: How are you faring this year, Paul?
Paul Wick: It has been a hard year for us. Although company fundamentals remain strong, our investments in the electronics industry have been buffeted by trade issues, particularly with regard to China. Also, investors’ infatuation with growth at any price has continued, and even strengthened. Shares of e-commerce companies such as Wayfair [ticker: W] and Shopify [SHOP] are well over $100, and the companies have yet to post positive earnings. The software group has done well; valuations have eclipsed their 2014 highs. It is pretty routine now for companies to trade for eight to 14 times revenue. There doesn’t seem to be much price discipline among investors.
We take it you don’t approve.
The information-technology spending environment overall is strong. That is apparent in the capital-spending plans of the so-called cloud titans— Google , Facebook [FB], Amazon.com [AMZN], and Microsoft [MSFT]. Their capital spending looks to be up about 40% in 2018. That is benefiting a big swath of semiconductor, software, and network-infrastructure companies, including Intel [INTC] and Micron Technology [MU], one of my January recommendations.
You predicted in January that some tech indexes would be up 15% or so this year. Do you still think that’s possible?
I do. There continues to be merger-and-acquisition activity in the industry, and technology arguably is the healthiest sector in the U.S. economy, and internationally. In addition to rising IT spending, the electronic content in automobiles has continued to increase. We also have more electric vehicles and hybrids on the road. The world is moving toward more data and faster data speeds. 5G networks are on the horizon, and will be rolled out over the next year, and a new Wi-Fi standard will start rolling out in 2019. The memory content in phones continues to increase. All of these trends are positive for technology stocks. With corporate profit margins so strong, the inclination to spend on IT will continue. The move to update applications and move more applications to the cloud shows no sign of slowing.
Paul Wick’s Report Card
What is the best way to invest in these trends?
Chip companies are the most inexpensive way to play cloud computing, greater computing power in mobile devices, faster data speeds, and higher semiconductor content in cars, plus the Internet of Things in factories and homes. I thought the semiconductor industry was undervalued in January, and it is still undervalued. The valuation gap relative to other areas of tech, especially the frothy growth names, is too big to ignore, and has only widened since January.
Broadcom [AVGO] is leveraged to the cloud. It is the leading supplier of Ethernet switch ICs [integrated circuits] and connectivity ICs in smartphones. It is also the leading ASICs [application-specific integrated circuit] vendor for AI-related chipsets. The stock went sideways in the past year due to substantial uncertainty surrounding the company’s attempted takeover of Qualcomm [QCOM]. [The deal was blocked by the Trump administration.] People also fretted about Broadcom’s exposure to Apple [AAPL], which accounts for about 15% of revenue. They worried that weak sales of Apple’s iPhone X would have a negative impact on Broadcom’s bulk acoustic-wave-filter business, and that has been the case; Broadcom has moderated its expectations for its Apple business.
This week Broadcom fell about 18%, to $207, on the surprising news that it has agreed to buy CA [CA], a software company.

Do you share Wall Street’s hostility to the deal?
The deal was a surprise, and the rationale was poorly communicated. Broadcom’s management feels the CA purchase is analogous to its acquisition last year of Brocade Communications Systems. Broadcom paid $5.9 billion for Brocade, but quickly divested Brocade’s lower-margin businesses for proceeds of $900 million. Importantly, Broadcom hung on to the crown jewels of Brocade—its Fiber Channel SAN [storage area network] switch assets—and boosted Brocade’s Ebitda [earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization] from $500 million last year to a projected $1.1 billion for 2018. So, a $5 billion outlay is now generating more than $1 billion per year in cash flow.
Broadcom sees CA as a similarly misunderstood set of assets— a mainframe and enterprise software business with exceptional profitability ensconced within a company desperate to show growth by investing in inferior businesses. The game plan will be to divest some of these less profitable businesses and cut costs, shrinking revenue from $4.2 billion to $3.5 billion, but boosting Ebitda from $1.6 billion to $2.5 billion. Broadcom has met or exceeded its expectations with every acquisition it has done, and appears confident of its ability to do so with CA.
Assuming $18 billion in new debt at a 3.9% borrowing cost, it is feasible that Broadcom’s CA deal could add well over $1 billion in incremental free cash flow for shareholders, or more than $2 per share. While we are frustrated with the manner in which the company communicated the logic behind the CA deal, the logic is sound. Inevitably, the investment community will better understand the company’s strategy and appreciate the quality of its high-margin businesses. How many public companies can aspire to 55% Ebitda margins? Very few, and that level of profitability is deserving of a much better valuation than 9-10 times enterprise value to free cash flow. Broadcom intends to continue returning 50% of free cash flow as dividends to shareholders, so we expect the dividend to increase steadily over time. The stock yields 3.4%.
How is the rest of Broadcom doing?
The rest of the business is doing well, especially on the infrastructure side, which is critical to data-center and cloud capital spending. In the fiscal quarter ended in April, Broadcom’s gross profit margin surprised to the upside, at 66.6%. The operating profit margin was 48.9%. Investors think Broadcom is just a mergers-and-acquisitions story, but they are missing the point.
I also like Integrated Device Technology [IDTI]. Its biggest business is memory buffers that go into servers. It has an 80% market share. Integrated Device is well positioned for cloud spending. In addition, microprocessor companies Intel [INTC] and Advanced Micro Devices [AMD] are introducing new server CPUs [central processing units] that accommodate more memory. As a result, the average selling price of Integrated Device’s memory buffers is going up. The company is ahead of plan on margin expansion, and has an aggressive share-repurchase program in place. The other parts of the business—industrial and automotive sensors, and wireless charging—are all growing nicely. People think that anything handset-related is problematic because the mobile phone market is flat, but wireless charging is just getting adopted.
How is the stock doing?
IDTI isn’t expensive. Shares trade for $34. The company could earn $1.90 to $2 a share in fiscal 2019 [ending next March]. It has a market value of around $4.5 billion, a size that would make it an attractive acquisition candidate for a lot of companies. Japan’s Renesas Electronics [6723.Japan], Broadcom, Skyworks Solutions [SWKS], and even Texas Instruments [TXN] could be buyers.
There are a lot of ways to win with Integrated Device. The company raised its revenue guidance for fiscal 2019 after reporting results for the March quarter. It entered the new fiscal year with exceptional new product and new customer strength and expects continued above-market revenue growth, coupled with further margin improvement. Annual revenue is around $900 million. The operating profit margin is 29%-30%. We think the stock could go to $40.
I also have two short ideas, both Canadian companies.
Tell us more.
The first is Canopy Growth [CGC], a producer of marijuana products. There are about 75 publicly traded cannabis companies in Canada, with more than $30 billion in market value. Canopy is the largest by market cap, at roughly $6 billion. These companies are losing a lot of money. Investors seem to think the industry eventually will become an oligopoly, with three or four companies generating 40% to 50% profit margins, not unlike cigarette companies. That view is misguided. It is fashionable to believe that Canadian companies will dominate the global marijuana industry. People are missing the fact that there is a huge black market.
There is a difference between branded cigarette companies and tobacco farmers. Canopy is a farming company. While branded companies get high profit margins, farmers have low profit margins and a lot of competition. Canopy sells almost all of its products to Canadian provincial governments for resale in state-owned stores. It is hard to build a branded consumer-products company when you are a pawn with no pricing power in a government revenue scheme. There is massive overcapacity in the business. All of these companies have raised big sums of money to prepare for the big bang of legalization in Canada. The total available market is going to prove to be small relative to the industry’s market cap.
Are you shorting Canopy only, or a basket of these stocks?
This is the only one in which we have a short position in our long/short strategy. Canopy’s Canadian shares [WEED.Canada] were selling for C$10 Canadian a year ago. The stock is now C$38.83. On a trailing 12-month basis, revenue was C$78 million. Free cash flow was negative C$280 million. The company just announced it was acquiring two companies to enter the Colombian and Latin American medicinal-marijuana markets. Both transactions were in shares. Canopy’s spending and deal making have boosted its share count from 124 million in April 2017 to an estimated 230 million as of June 30. [A Canopy Growth spokesman told Barron’s that equity transactions are more common in the cannabis industry because access to capital is more challenging. He said the company aims to have positive free cash flow this year.]
Shopify also has had extraordinarily successful share appreciation despite the company’s modest bottom-line results. Shopify’s software enables small businesses to sell products online. The company has a market value of $16 billion and is expected to generate revenue this year of $1 billion. It trades for 15-16 times revenue. Earnings and cash flow are break-even.
Shopify has rallied about 400% in the past two years. Why such exuberance?
We are in an environment where people care only about top-line revenue growth. Meanwhile, great companies in semiconductor land that are generating huge profits get rewarded with pedestrian multiples. Many of Shopify’s customers are small-time entrepreneurs using the platform to drop-ship products sourced in China. They advertise products on social-media sites such as Facebook and Instagram. About 65% of the Shopify customer base has been with the company for a year or less. Only 123,000 of 765,000 Shopify domains have meaningful traffic. There is a large amount of churn within the company’s installed base. Two things could prove problematic, in addition to valuation.
What are they?
One is that Facebook is under pressure to clean up its site and get rid of low-quality advertisers about whom users have complained. As Facebook scrubs its advertising over the next year, that could be negative for Shopify. [A Shopify spokeswoman said the platform isn’t tied to any one channel.] The second issue has to do with postal costs. The U.S. has a postal agreement called ePacket that governs certain shipping costs and has allowed Chinese e-commerce merchants to ship goods to the U.S. extremely cheaply. We believe that agreement expired June 30. I don’t know how or when this will play out. The business could prove to be more fragile than it looks.
Can you update your January picks?
Sure. Micron has continued to post strong results. Margins have expanded. The company has cleaned up its balance sheet and announced a $10 billion share repurchase to commence on Sept. 1. The stock is doing well. Western Digital [WDC] put up good results, but the stock has gone sideways. People are worried that NAND flash memory prices are going down. I’m not; prices usually go down. The company’s per-bit production costs are also going down, and profitability remains consistent. Plus, the hard-drive business is booming. Western Digital is on track to earn around $14 this year, and the stock is $77.
Marvell Technology Group [MRVL] won approval from Chinese regulators to purchase Cavium, and the transaction closed in early July. The deal is highly accretive to earnings. On its own, Marvell has been reporting good results. Oracle [ORCL] reported two mildly disappointing quarters. The shares have underperformed the software group and the broad market. We believe the company is largely on track. Oracle has been aggressive about repatriating offshore cash and buying back shares. It bought back $11 billion of stock in the latest fiscal year. Oracle is on track for 3% to 4% constant-currency revenue growth in fiscal 2019, and 10% earnings-per-share growth, bolstered by a lower share count.
Snap [SNAP], the parent of Snapchat, is down 10% since the January Roundtable. Will the selling continue?
The stock rose sharply in February after the company reported above-consensus fourth-quarter revenue. Then it tanked on disappointing March-quarter results and June guidance delivered in early May. Specifically, daily-active-user numbers declined sequentially in the U.S. and globally, and time spent on the platform fell. SNAP’s redesign of its app turned off users and notable celebrities. The company reported negative free cash flow of $268 million for the March quarter. We remain bearish on the company and the stock.
Intrexon [XON], another short recommendation, is up a bit. After our January Roundtable meeting the company raised an additional $87 million to bolster its balance sheet. The stock then rallied on good fourth-quarter revenue but later fell on weak first-quarter revenue, continued losses, and a delay in a Phase 1 glioblastoma drug trial. Intrexon continues to lose roughly $150 million a year, and recently announced another money raise for $200 million in convertible debt. We remain bearish on the company and its outstanding securities.
Thank you, Paul.
